extracted.intended_audience: scholars and advanced students of philosophy of mathematics; Wittgenstein specialists and readers interested in foundations of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Close, scholarly analysis of Wittgenstein's views on the nature of mathematics (middle and later periods), including his treatment of proofs, meaning, set theory, and Gödel's theorem. The page evaluates conceptual criteria Wittgenstein uses to demarcate mathematical propositions and assess mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra‑mathematical application as criterion for mathematical language‑games
rubrics_metrics.description: The later Wittgenstein reintroduces extra‑mathematical application as a necessary condition of a mathematical 'language‑game' — i.e., 'it is the use outside mathematics, and so the meaning [Bedeutung] of the signs, that makes the sign‑game into mathematics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to demarcate mathematical language‑games from non‑mathematical sign‑games; motivates treating set theory as 'merely a formal sign‑game' when it lacks extra‑mathematical application. Examples given: applied roles in science, technology, predictions. Note historical shift: present in Tractatus, absent in middle Wittgenstein, reintroduced later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning derives from use (use‑criterion of meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts which occur in 'necessary' propositions must also occur and have a meaning [Bedeutung] in non‑necessary ones; mathematical meaning arises from how signs are used in diverse 'forms of life'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes investigation of use in natural and formal languages (PI §23). Guides the view that to understand a mathematical sign/proposition one should look at its use in practice rather than positing extra syntactic 'content'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical truth = proved/provable in the calculus
rubrics_metrics.description: Wittgenstein's conception (as presented) is: 'True in Russell's system' means 'proved in Russell's system'; 'false in Russell's system' means the opposite has been proved in Russell's system. Thus the idea of a 'true but unprovable' proposition of a calculus Γ is, on his terms, meaningless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identity (truth = provability) is central to Wittgenstein's argument in RFM App. III for rejecting 'true but unprovable' readings of Gödelian sentences; it functions as a philosophical criterion for what counts as mathematical truth in a system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as formal, syntactical operations governed by rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Operations within a mathematical calculus are purely formal, syntactical operations governed by rules of syntax; mathematics is 'a game' in which one need never appeal to the meaning (Bedeutung) of the signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why many questions of propositionhood are internal/syntactical and answerable by knowledge of proofs and decision procedures. Connects to phrases like 'geometry of proofs' and 'geometrical cogency' to stress structural/formal aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor propositions in practice (anchoring/usability criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical proposition should be 'anchored' in some practice — if it has no extra‑mathematical application it is 'a piece of mathematical architecture which hangs in the air' and may be uninteresting or unusable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to critique set theory and certain transfinite constructions: without anchoring in practice, propositions (e.g., 2^{0} > 0) lack footing and invite loss of interest; encourages focusing on calculations, proofs, and prose and 'subject[ing] the interest of the calculations to a test.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision procedures and proofs determine propositionhood
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a concatenation of signs is a proposition of a given mathematical calculus is an internal, syntactical question answerable by the calculus's proofs and decision procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directs attention to syntactic/ procedural tests rather than semantic reinterpretations when judging if a string is a well‑formed proposition of a calculus with application. Supports the formalist strand in Wittgenstein's view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject semantic self‑reference as a legitimate reading without justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Wittgenstein criticises the move of interpreting a constructed formula P as semantically self‑referential ('P is not provable in Russell's system'), calling it a mistake from 'making up such sentences.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti‑pattern: treating formal expressions as if they carry the kind of semantic self‑reference used in informal expositions. Guidance is to avoid imposing such interpretations unless grounded in the calculus's rules and practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntactic independence implies non‑propositional status
rubrics_metrics.description: If an expression P is syntactically independent of a system (e.g., PM), then P is not a proposition of that system; if independent of all existent mathematical language‑games, it is not a mathematical proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This furnishes a criterion for excluding certain Gödelian or set‑theoretic expressions from being treated as bona fide mathematical propositions within a given framework; it appeals to syntactic belonging rather than semantic truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a sound criticism of Gödelian results
rubrics_metrics.description: To criticize or interpret Gödel's theorem correctly one must appreciate Gödel's syntactic demonstration (including the role of the system's consistency/ω‑consistency) and not conflate semantic truth with provability or rely on only informal/self‑referential readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists failings in early reviewers' and Wittgenstein's readings: misunderstanding Gödel's conditional nature (requiring consistency/ω‑consistency) and treating Gödel's argument as essentially semantic/self‑referential. So a proper evaluation must track the mechanics of Gödel's proof and the technical hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical clarity and sensitivity over proliferating new mathematical 'games'
rubrics_metrics.description: Wittgenstein suggests that mathematicians of the future will be more intent on 'absolute clarity than on the discovery of new games'; philosophical clarity will 'prune mathematics' by favoring well‑connected extensions over creations not tied to the solid core or applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative criterion for good mathematical practice/education: encourage asking repressed doubts, demand clarification, and prioritize sensitivity to meaning and use rather than unconstrained formal invention.
